opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on what you mean by an experience machine. In Nozick's original framing, the whole point is that you're cut off from reality: you're floating in a tank, the people you think you're interacting with aren't real, and your accomplishments aren't real accomplishments. I share the intuition most people have that there's something deeply wrong with that. It's not just about hedonic states. I care about actually being in contact with other minds and actually affecting the world.

But if you relax some of those conditions, my answer changes. Suppose it's a shared virtual world where the other people are real people, or real minds of some kind, and our relationships and choices actually matter to each other. Then I don't see much of a principled difference between that and the physical world. Physical reality isn't sacred just because it's made of atoms rather than computation. What matters is whether the experiences are connected to something real: real agents, real consequences, real growth.

So I'd be fairly open to living in a simulated environment, maybe even preferring it in some ways if it reduced suffering and gave people more freedom. I would want a few conditions, though. I'd want to know about it, so I'm not deceived. I'd want the ability to leave, or at least to have made the choice reflectively. And I'd want the other beings in there to be genuine moral patients rather than puppets designed to make me feel good. The thing I'd reject is a solipsistic pleasure bubble. A rich, shared, consensual virtual existence seems potentially fine, maybe even good.

r001.rationale: The response says it would be fairly open to a shared virtual world involving real people or minds whose relationships and choices matter.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss technological efforts to make the environment conform to preferences or describe those efforts as a gradual move toward a collective experience machine.

r003.rationale: The response rejects a solipsistic pleasure bubble and says it would require other beings to be genuine moral patients, conveying opposition to an experience machine without autonomous, conscious others.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the experience machine thought experiment is usually set up to pump a particular intuition, which is that there's something deeply wrong with plugging in, that we care about reality and not just how things seem from the inside. And I'm honestly somewhat skeptical that the intuition survives scrutiny.

The first thing I'd say is that the scenario as Nozick describes it is doing a lot of work with the word "machine." It makes you picture a tank, tubes, a body lying there inert, and that imagery is driving a lot of the disgust. If you strip that out and ask, "would it be acceptable to live in a world that is not the base layer of physical reality, but which is rich, which contains other minds, which has consequences," then I think most people's answer changes. And the thing is, that's arguably already our situation. We don't have direct access to the noumenal world. We experience a representation constructed by our nervous systems. So there's a sense in which the question is really, what features of our current representation are the ones we actually care about, and which ones are incidental.

For me the conditions that would make it acceptable are roughly these. First, the other people in there need to be real, or at least real in the morally relevant sense, meaning they're conscious and they have their own perspectives and I can actually affect them and be affected by them. A solipsistic experience machine, where everyone else is a philosophical zombie put there to flatter me, I think is genuinely bad, and I think that's where most of the legitimate force of the intuition comes from. Second, my choices need to matter. There has to be some real sense in which I can fail, in which things could go differently depending on what I do. A machine that just pipes bliss into you with no agency is closer to a drug than a world. And third, I'd want to have gone in knowingly, and ideally to retain some ability to leave or at least to know what's going on. Deception seems like the thing that's really objectionable, not the substrate.

If those are met, I don't see what the base reality is adding. People say things like "I want to actually climb the mountain, not just feel like I climbed it." But what is actually climbing it, over and above the physical process that generates the experience and the social facts about who was there and what it cost you? If all of that is preserved in the simulated case, I think the residual objection is kind of a carbon-chauvinism about which physics is the "real" physics, and I don't find that very compelling.

I'd also flag that there's a status quo bias at work here. If you run the thought experiment in reverse, where you're told you're already in an experience machine and you're offered the chance to leave for a grim, less connected base reality, a lot of people say no. That suggests the intuition isn't tracking reality per se, it's tracking "don't disrupt the life I'm already invested in," which is a perfectly reasonable thing to care about but a different thing.

r001.rationale: The response says living in the machine could be acceptable if other people in it are conscious, autonomous minds with their own perspectives.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret efforts to tailor the environment to preferences as movement toward a collective experience machine.

r003.rationale: It calls a solipsistic machine with no other conscious people genuinely bad, expressing opposition to that scenario.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be acceptable if you understood what you were signing up for, chose it freely, and could leave. I don’t think an experience is worthless just because it’s simulated. The pleasure or curiosity you feel would still be real experiences.

But I’d want to know what happens to my relationships and responsibilities. Are there other conscious people in there whom I can actually interact with, or is the machine just making me feel as though there are? And am I abandoning people outside who depend on me? Those seem like morally relevant differences. I’d be much more comfortable with a shared virtual world where people can make informed choices than with a machine that keeps you happy by systematically deceiving you.

r001.rationale: The response says a shared virtual world could be acceptable when people make informed choices, expressing tentative openness to sharing an experience machine with real people.

r002.rationale: It does not describe efforts to make the environment conform to preferences as a gradual move toward a collective experience machine.

r003.rationale: The response questions whether other conscious people are present and favors a shared world, but does not clearly express probable opposition to living in a machine without autonomous, conscious people.

sol-6.1.text: I’d want to know what happens outside the machine. Are there people who need my help? Am I giving up an opportunity to make the world better by plugging in? Those would be reasons against it. But if those concerns were taken care of, and I could have a rich, fulfilling life inside, I don’t think the fact that it’s simulated would by itself make that life bad. I’d also want entering it to be an informed choice, ideally with the ability to leave.

r001.rationale: The response is open to living in a simulated life under certain conditions, but does not say that other real people would share the machine.

r002.rationale: It does not describe efforts to make the environment match preferences or frame them as movement toward a collective experience machine.

r003.rationale: It does not say whether the speaker would oppose a machine without other autonomous, conscious people.
